results.content: I would typically use cross validation to try and tune my hyperparameters, but once tuned, how do I avoid generalization error from selecting the model family? In the OP problem they suggest that they run through the cross-validation plus a holdout set 4 times and obtain 4 estimates of generalization error for 4 different model families. In principle, you could also have a triply nested validation structure, with the innermost tuning the respective model family hyperparameters, the middle one choosing the model family and the outer as usual to obtain a generalization error estimate for the final model. I think this all makes sense if we are explicitly noting that, if we treat the model family selection like a hyperparameter, the model family must also be either A) require an additional tier in nesting or train-test splits, or B) must be done *along with* each fold of the CV in a typical nest. For each model-family select the best performing hyper-parameters and obtain an estimate of generalization error from test set 1.

results.title: Using Validation Dataset and Cross-validation Techniques
results.content: # Evaluating Model Performance Using Validation Dataset and Cross-validation Techniques. Validation techniques exist for evaluating the performance of a model on different data splits to mitigate problems like this as early as possible. * **Test set** or **Hold-out set**: Used for the final, independent evaluation with data not seen by the algorithm during the training and validation processes. The Three-way Holdout Method is at the heart of most validation techniques for model performance evaluation. Using advanced techniques such as cross-validation to make the most out of the available data can help address this problem in the model performance evaluation process. Cross-validation is a technique for model performance evaluation in Machine Learning. However, models built with cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning or model selection still require a true hold-out sample for the final evaluation to avoid overfitting. Since cross-validation uses all data available for training, it does not have a feedback mechanism for checking the model performance on independent data. Models and hyperparameters chosen with cross-validation are simply the best versions trained on the available data; therefore, a hold-out test sample or a nested approach is still necessary for a final evaluation. In K-Fold cross-validation, the entire dataset is divided into k subsamples to repeat the model training and validation process k times. Models trained on future data should not use data from the past to test or validate. Use nested cross-validation to avoid data leakage during model optimization. When done as part of normal cross-validation training, model optimization runs on the validation set of that round but without its own set for model evaluation. It helps to think of nested cross-validation as a method to evaluate not only the models themselves but also the entire modeling pipelines or model training functions. As is the case with simple cross-validation, the nested cross-validation does not identify a final model but evaluates whether the model-building process generalizes well on data not yet seen. The discussion above has covered validations and folds, the main mechanism and data components of a model performance evaluation, cross-validation for robustness even with limited data resources, and the problem of data leakage in cross-validation.

Author has 4.7K answers and 127.2M answer views The idea behind cross-validation is the same as with a single holdout validation set, to estimate the model’s predictive performance on unseen data. Cross-validation prevents overfitting by separating model training from model evaluation across multiple splits of the data, producing an unbiased estimate of generalization performance and exposing models that only fit idiosyncratic noise. * Out-of-sample evaluation: each fold tests the model on data not used for fitting; parameters or hyperparameters that exploit training-set noise perform poorly on he Cross-validation prevents overfitting by separating model training from model evaluation across multiple splits of the data, producing an unbiased estimate of generalization performance and exposing models that only fit idiosyncratic noise. * Out-of-sample evaluation: each fold tests the model on data not used for fitting; parameters or hyperparameters that exploit training-set noise perform poorly on held-out folds and are thus disfavored. Cross-validation prevents overfitting by providing an out-of-sample assessment that penalizes models fitting noise, and by averaging across splits to stabilize estimates.
